utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Everybody is in his position. Good morning to the interpreters. We can now resume our work with the testimony of the next witness. Mr. Nobilo or Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honour. This morning, our first witness will be quite brief, but it is necessary to call this witness in closed session, and I can give further explanation, but I would ask to do that also in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Prosecutor have any objections? I know it's always a sensitive issue because we're asking for a closed session without really knowing why, but we have to have a closed session to find out why. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've stated the position, Mr. President, so I have nothing to add to what you've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can move into closed session so we can have an explanation as to why we need a closed session. A completely closed session or a private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Completely closed session. I can give my explanation in private, but the witness would need to be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We'll make things simpler. We'll simply have a completely closed session with the agreement of counsel. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume our work now. Have the accused brought in. No, the accused is already here. There is no problem, so we can resume. Where are we, Mr. Registrar? Are we going to hear the testimony of another witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence has to tell us that there is going to be another witness in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. And then after that we can see what we are going to do with the previous witness. All right. Mr. Nobilo, this is apparently not a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just, actually, a point of order. If I could introduce to the Court, Mr. Simon Hooper, who will be our case manager, the gentleman on my left. I know we've had a number of people coming through as case manager. I think Mr. Hooper will be with us until the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think I can speak for Judge Shahabuddeen by welcoming your assistant, although I didn't quite catch his name. Mr. Hooper -- yes, I see it on the monitor. Mr. Hooper. Welcome, Mr. Hooper. Welcome to this Trial Chamber. Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next witness is Mrs. Ivanka Valenta. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are going to tell us your name, your first name, the date and place of your birth, your profession, your current residence, and then you are going to take an oath. All right. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone wasn't on. The interpreters couldn't hear the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an assistant worker at the public library and I live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (No translation) All right. All right. Is it working now? Does anybody hear me? Just stop for a moment, please. Let me begin again. All right. Excuse me. Please repeat your name, your first name, the date and place of your birth, your current place of residence, and if you have a profession, tell us what it is, and then you will take an oath. And then after that you will be seated. All right, so first name, date and place of birth and your current residence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivanka Valenta, born on the 6th of April, 1964, in Poculice, employed as an assistant worker at the public library in Vitez, where I also live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take the oath now by reading the statement which is on the piece of paper the usher has given you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. You may now be seated. The Tribunal thanks you for having come to participate in the trial of General Blaskic, who at the time of the alleged facts was a Colonel. He is in the courtroom to your left. You are going to answer the Defence Counsel's questions because the Defence is the one who brought you here, and then the opposing party will ask questions, that is the Office of the Prosecutor, and, perhaps, Judges questions as well. Mr. Nobilo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, I would like to have a document distributed, a map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D519.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the document is being distributed, you said you were born in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: No, in Poculice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me where you got married and where you lived before the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: I got married in Kruscica, and I lived there for 11 years before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court -- rather, look at this map. You can see it on the monitor too. Is the village of Kruscica on this map?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see that the village of Kruscica is a very long, stretched out village. Tell me, which part of the village did you live in, near Vitez or the other part?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: No, at the other end of the Muslim part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the actual conflict, or before the 15th of April, did you notice something which now seems important to you?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: I noticed that BiH Army soldiers were dug in in the part of the forest near Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: This was immediately after the new year, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two days before the conflict did something happen which you were not aware of then, but now you know what it was all about?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Well, I happened to be going for a walk, this was during the Easter holidays, and I saw an unusual detail, a tractor going into the forest, and it was covered with twigs and branches. Because it was funny, usually you take branches out of the forest rather than into the forest. And two days later, when the fighting broke out, we concluded or, rather, I concluded on the basis of the detonations that I heard that these were weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us directly move onto the 15th of April, 1993, the day on the eve of the conflict, the war between the Croats and the Muslims in the Lasva River Valley. Tell me, where were you then and what did you notice? Could you please tell the Court about this.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: I was in the village in the house on the other side of the black house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Court what the black house is.

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: The black house is a camp from the Second World War which was used by the BiH Armies. I don't know what they used it for, but they spent quite a bit of time there, and we saw quite a few soldiers there. And around 3.00 in the afternoon I was supposed to go home, and I looked at it and there was an enormous number of soldiers there. At 1.00, as I was passing there, there was no one, and then I was really surprised at 3.00. And then we decided to wait and see what was going on. At first I thought that perhaps maybe they were gathering there because they wanted to go to Sarajevo to fight against the Serbs. However, since they remained there and the owner of the house that we were in looked through the window and he said that they are not only up there, but they are also at the other road too. And we waited there for about an hour, or two, we waited until about 5.00, and then we finally had to go home. And we had to pass that way. We had to. There was no other way to go. As we were passing by the gate of the yard of the black house, there was an enormous number of BiH Army soldiers and there was only one person among them from the neighbourhood whom I knew. And we said "hello" very nicely and nobody responded in any way. So we continued to our home truly frightened. Around 6.00 or 6.30 my husband had to go to work, and I did not dare stay at home on my own. And when it became dark, I went to the neighbouring house, which was closer to the HVO soldiers. And everything was quiet, nothing was happening, and around 2.00 my husband came and said that we had to withdraw because something was in the making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, before you continue, I would like to put a few questions to you at this juncture. You said that at 3.00 in the afternoon, until 5.00, when you left, in front of the black house where the BiH Army was there were two enormous groups of soldiers, you said?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Yes. One was in the yard around the black house, and the other one was at the lower road to Kruscica where the road leading to the so-called Glivara (phoen) is too. I can't remember the name of the owner. I can't remember his last name. There were a lot of people scattered about. You could really see that they were waiting for something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please speak a bit slower for purposes of interpretation, and we should also make small pauses between questions and answers. According to your assessment, how many soldiers were in every one of these two groups?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: In each group, there were at least a hundred men, according to my assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know your Muslim neighbours who were in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Territorial Defence. Were they foreign soldiers or were they local soldiers? How would you define them?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: I only recognised two of them. One is Ahmic, I don't remember his first name, and the other is my next door neighbour, Ibrahim Hidic, and I don't know anyone else. All of them were unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, around your house, were there some barricades, roadblocks, that were put up that evening?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that evening when my husband came to the house where I was staying, he said that there were roadblocks near our house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who put up these roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: The BH army. I didn't take anything along. I just put my jacket on my shoulders. I didn't even take my ID or anything, although we all did have something prepared, like, we had bags packed because we were afraid of the air force at that time, and I didn't even go home to get some warmer clothes. Actually, I wanted to but my husband wouldn't let me, and he said that there were roadblocks in front of our house made of rocks and big tyres that are used for trucks, and a hundred metres away towards the Croatian houses --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us recall what this is. We are talking about the evening of the 15th of April, so this is before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Yes, before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you definitely leave your house?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: At 6.30, at 6.30 p.m. on the 15th, and I didn't go back there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: We went to the house of Lojza Miskovic, perhaps 500 metres closer to HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you leave the house of Lojza Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: On the 16th in the morning at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: We went to a building called Lovac where HVO soldiers were stationed, and we sought safety there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many HVO soldiers were at Lovac?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: My estimate was about 15. I didn't really count them, but there were very few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that? When did the shooting start and how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: We came there at 4.00, and, well, we were afraid, and we all went to the basement. And I think that it was at 6.00 that we felt the first detonation, and the building that we were in had quite a bit of glass, perhaps a quarter of the building was in glass, and the glass shattered, and there was panic all over. Shooting broke out, and I personally thought that we would not live to see the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this shooting directed at the Lovac Hotel where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, definitely, and we should give credit where it's due. Not a single shell missed its target. None of them missed their target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point in time during a brief lull in the shooting on the 16th of April, you peeked and saw part of your house. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: We were staying in the basement, and there was no water there and there wasn't a toilet, and it is only human that we had to relieve ourselves. So I had to find some place that could serve as a toilet, and I found an ironing board in part of this basement, and I climbed up to this ironing board so that I could see through the window what was going on outside, and I could see my house. I could see two men at the front door who -- they got out of my house carrying the TV set, and they were taking it to the house next door, and I was so hurt by this that I couldn't bear watching this anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they manage to get close to the Lovac Hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: No, not in daytime, but when night fell, they came only 100 metres away, and one soldier got in, and he wanted to activate a grenade amongst us. He was panic-stricken, and he said, "We're finished. They are only 100 metres away from us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldier you're talking about was one of the HVO soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did you manage to escape? Could you please describe this to the Court?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Behind this building in part of the forest, there was a water installation, waterworks, and there were also seven Croat houses, and sometimes before that during the night, somebody would, for example, turn off the water, and then the waterpipes would freeze and then we would all have problem with the water, and this was the only way through which the BH army could reach us, that side, from the waterworks. And that night, there was no light, no nothing, and this soldier didn't want to turn on the lights, and this area was mined, but he managed to demine it, and then we went there, went through this area, on the morning of the 17th at 4.00 in the morning, escorted by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now we're going to finish describing these events. After the war, did you manage to go back to your house in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: No, no, in my house in Kruscica, there is a family from Veceriska. They are living there now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your property?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: My property, the property from all our houses, to the best of our knowledge and according to what I saw and according to what some of the Croats told us who remained imprisoned for a month, all the houses were looted on that very same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That would be all, Mr. President. This concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You went right to the essentials. Mr. Dubuisson, I suppose you've got a number for the card.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. This would be 519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 519. Mr. Cayley -- no, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment, Mr. President? Mr. Harmon wants to speak with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Valenta. My name is Cayley. I'm from the Office of the Prosecutor. This is my colleague, Mr. Harmon. I only have a few questions for you. Now, you stated on the 15th of April that you were passing through Kruscica and you made a number of observations. Now, can you tell me where the school is in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: I did not say that I was passing through Kruscica, through the whole village, but that I was on the opposite side of the black house, the crna kuca, because my house is up above, and I came in from the opposite side, from the black house side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where the school is in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: In the middle of the Muslim part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 14th or 15th of April, did you have occasion to pass the school at Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated, I think, that on the morning of the 16th of April, you went to the Hotel Lovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time was that?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you to go to the Hotel Lovac?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: My husband came to the house where we were, and he said that we should withdraw amongst the HVO soldiers for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Croats withdrew to the Hotel Lovac?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Nineteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're aware that the Hotel Lovac was an HVO military headquarters, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: I know that the HVO army was there, but what it actually was, I don't know. I'm not acquainted with military matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand that. Now, can you tell the Court what time the conflict began?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Six a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Valenta, are you aware that the HVO commenced an attack in Vitez and Ahmici at 5.30 in the morning on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVANKA VALENTA
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't even know what my name was at the time. Ahmici is a long way away from the part in which I live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much, Ms. Valenta. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn to Judge Shahabuddeen. There won't be any further questions. Thank you for having come, Ms. Valenta. Excuse me, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's true there was a cross-examination. All right. Thank you, Ms. Valenta, for having come to The Hague to testify. We wish you Godspeed back to your country, and the usher will escort you out of the courtroom. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, Mr. Hayman, the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next witness is Andzelka Matic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me look in the notes that were given to me. All right. Andzelka Matic, yes, yes, I have it here. All right. We can have the witness brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Madam? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please tell us your name, your first name, your date and place of birth, your profession, if you have one, and your current residence, and then please remain standing for a few more moments, as long as it takes to take an oath. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Andzelka Matic. I was born on the 16th of October, 1951 in the village of Gacice which is where I now live, and I'm a housewife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Would you take the oath, please, reading the declaration which the usher is going to give you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. You may be seated now. You have agreed to testify at the request of the Defence in the trial initiated by the Office of the Prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal against General Blaskic who, at the time, was a Colonel and who is in this courtroom on your left. First, you will be asked some questions by those who had you come, that is, the accused's Defence counsel and then questions from the Office of the Prosecutor, if there are any, and possibly questions from the Judges. Mr. Nobilo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, you lived and live in Gacice. By profession, you're a housewife. You're married and the mother of two children?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague has been signalling to me to tell me that, although you and I speak the same language, we should slow down a little. So when I ask you the question, make a slight pause, and then give us your answer. I should like to hand out a map at this point for you to identify your village.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D520.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are going to see in front of you on the ELMO a map which shows Vitez and a red arrow. Does the arrow depict your village correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, is your village near the military explosives factory?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how big is it? How many houses is the village comprised of?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: There are about 100 houses. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ratio of the population between the Muslim and Croat households? How many of one, how many of the other?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I would say it was about half/half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you form village watches of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they uni-national or were they Croat and Muslim village watches?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: They were Croat/Muslim watches jointly set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until what time? When were these village watches separated?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The village watches were jointly manned up until the time when the Muslims, overnight, stole two anti-aircraft guns which were positioned at our cemetery because of the Serbian aviation which had launched an assault on our factory on one occasion, and since the time that the guns were stolen, the village watches became separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take the guns, the Muslims from your village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The guns were taken to Vitez, to the section that they refer to as the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to April 1993. Tell us, on the eve of the conflict, how do you assess relationships between the Croat population of the village and the Muslim neighbours? What were the relationships like?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: As far as incidents are concerned, there weren't any. In view of the circumstances, that is to say, there was general tension, and people were restless and divided. Some people would say hello to one another, others wouldn't. Everybody was in a general state of panic as to what would be in store for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were no incidents or conflicts, as you say?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, no incidents, no conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now move directly towards the events. On the day of the 15th of April, 1993 which is the day before the conflict broke out in the Vitez municipality between the Croats and Muslims, some people will say that the Croats, others say that the Muslims attacked, what information did you receive on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive any kind of information at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe to us now what the 16th of April, 1993 looked like? What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, shooting could already be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: In Donja Veceriska which is the village across the road from our factory. On one side, you have the village of Gacice and on the opposite side is Donja Veceriska, a village we can see quite well, and as it's fairly close, we could hear shooting and see smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your own village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The people were panicking, and in my own village, people began, quite simply, to talk to each other to decide what they were going to do, and our people decided to assign one man who would be a sort of commander in the village on the Croat side, and this was also done by the Muslims. They also appointed a man of their own to represent their side. And so our people sent this man, the man who had been elected from amongst us, to negotiate with the Muslims, and we tried to reach decisions on two or three occasions, agreements, but they were not successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on the 16th of April, the 17th, 18th of April, right up until the 20th of April, was there any shooting in your village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could they not agree upon, the two representatives, the Croat and the Muslim representatives from your villages?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, both sides asked that arms be surrendered. The Croats asked the Muslims to surrender their arms, and the Muslims asked us to do so, and they did not reach any agreement on that score.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So between the 16th and 20th of April, there was no fighting in your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, 1993, what happened on that particular day? Could you describe this for the benefit of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of April at around 7.00, I heard two to three strong detonations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in your house at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed that a conflict would break out?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, we had no information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in your house with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was in the house with my two daughters, and my husband's brother was there, he's an elderly man, a pensioner, and his wife, my brother and sister-in-law with their three small children. We would often gather there in my own house because we had a basement, and we used to do this because of the Serbs and because of the factory. We were afraid that they might use their planes to attack the factory, and we were safest there. And as the situation was generally tense with the Muslims as well, we would, out of simple fear, all collect there. Several families would be in a house with a basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see on that particular day from the morning onwards? What do you remember of it?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, after those two or three strong detonations, there was a lull. When I went out of the basement and looked through the kitchen window, I saw smoke at the end of the village, I did not know what it was, and after the lull, shooting started from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, up until noon, you spent that time in the basement.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you leave the basement from time to time to see what the situation was like in the village around your house?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, did you look towards the house of Fabijan Matic, a Croat, your brother-in-law? What was happening there?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps in the second hour of the shooting I saw smoke. It is my brother-in-law's house, Fabijan Matic, which was already on fire, and I saw three men, my next door neighbour, it is the brother of Marko Matic who was in the basement, and I saw standing by the window three men. I tried to recognise them. I saw their checkerboard insignia on their caps. I thought it was one of ours. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they doing? Describe this for us?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: When they were standing by the window, my brother-in-law's house began to burn, the shed which is right next to the house and the barn as well. And they went out onto the road and moved along the road and they had a cannister, an oranged coloured cannister in their hands, and when they walked along the road they were passing my own house, and at that particular moment the shooting stopped from the Muslim section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go on, when you saw this cannister, what is a cannister usually used for, the orange coloured cannister? What did you think?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought they were carrying some inflammable liquid, petrol or gas or something, and they used it for setting things alight. When they drew close, I went out and stood at the door, more out of panic and fear than inquisitiveness, in order to recognise them. I saw that they did have a checkerboard insignia on their foreheads, but that they weren't Croats because I recognised the Muslims who were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us their names? Who do you recognise exactly?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Two of them were the sons of Ramulj Hamdija. I don't know their names exactly. One of them was the son of Avdo Herceg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was burning at that time of the Croatian buildings which you could see from your front door?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: My brother-in-law's house was on fire, Fabijan's house was burning, and Ivo Matic, my other brother-in-law's house, had started to burn, and Marko Matic's house. So the first house next door to me is Marko, and then Ivan and Fabijan, they are both brothers of my husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What of Marko Matic's property was on fire?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, two of his buildings were on fire. The house had started to catch alight, but only the windows, the curtains, part of the carpet was on fire. But the whole of the shed and the barn were burnt and the horse, the cow, the calf, they were all burnt. And the pig.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to the events. These three men who set alight the house approached you. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: They stopped for a while and when I peeped through the front door they cursed my ustashas mother and said, "Well, you see that we are very good shots." I didn't quite understand the word that they were using, but I think that they shot at me with a sniper from Serif Hrustic's house. And I was lucky it was one or two centimeters off, away from my head, so that I -- just bits and pieces went into my eyes, and I went into the house and didn't leave it after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear something happening again? What time was this and what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, the shooting went on for about five or six -- until about 5.00 or 6.00, towards evening, I don't know exactly. But at that time I heard somebody shouting, "Left wing forward. We are winning."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you come to realise later on? Who had come and who shouted this?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I went to the window once again and I saw that it was our army, because they were not far off from my own house. There is a crossroads there. And after a brief space of time a group of Muslims went out carrying a white flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear? How did the fighting cease? The one surrendered with the white flag. Did all of them surrender?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: It was one group. Another group went towards the lower part of the village also carrying a flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody succeed in escaping?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The Muslims who had been fighting and had carried weapons went out towards the upper half of the village and the forest towards Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO intentionally leave them this space to pass through?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you went out and the fighting had ceased, what did you do? What was your first concern?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: When I went out, I saw that the shed and barn was on fire, that is to say some of my brother's facilities. This was by his house and it is about 100 metres off from my own house. I went outside. Two soldiers came. I did not know them, but I asked them, "May we go and put the fire out to stop the house from burning down, put the fire out with these other two facilities?" And the two soldiers gave us permission to do so. So we went out, we put out the fire. We broke down the roof of the summer kitchen to stop the rest of the house from burning down. And I did this until nightfall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next few days, or perhaps on that particular day, did you see any of the Muslim houses burning?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where, in what part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The Muslim houses were burnt down in what we call the old part of the village, the centre of the village, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your assessment, how many Muslim houses had burnt down?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I think between 10 and 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of the total of the 50 or so houses that you said existed in the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the casualties were from the conflict, what you heard and saw? What were the casualties on both sides?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard, when I went with that soldier out to put out the fire and to help my brother put out the fire, I asked him whether there were any casualties, and he said that one Croatian soldier had been killed and that his name was Marko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I heard that one young man had been killed who had started to flee, and that he was killed by a Muslim, Hrustic Nasir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear this from the Muslims or from the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, both sides talked about that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other casualties?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: One Muslim was burnt alive in his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: It was Hrustic Fikret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this happen? What did you hear about that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I heard that Croats called out to him and asked him to come out of the house, but, quite simply, he either did not wish to do so or did not dare do so. And that man used drink a lot, so that our people thought that he was probably drunk at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he otherwise a well loved man? Did the Croats like him too?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was a very nice man, a very fine man, and we all liked him. He liked to joke, he played the harmonica, he was a builder by profession, he worked at my house and he worked for my brother, and everybody respected him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those two people died, the young man who fled and was killed by the Muslims, and Fikret Hrustic who was killed in his house. The Croats called him, but he did not leave the house. Were there any other casualties on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, Herceg Ekrem, I think his name was, died upon exiting the village. I don't know who killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those are three victims. What about anybody else? Were there any more casualties?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, one other person was killed perhaps due to shelling. A grenade got him. Yes. The other was -- his surname was Hrustic, I don't remember his name, but he was killed by a grenade in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of these four individuals, to the best of your knowledge, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with the Muslim civilians? You said that two groups surrendered. Were they men, soldiers who had surrendered in those two groups?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the men taken?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, they were all taken together to Vitez, but they returned quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the men return or just the women, children and the elderly return?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I think that everybody returned, except those who went on towards Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit that part of the village when the Muslims returned? Is it close to your house or further off from your own house?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, when the Muslims returned, they were put up in a couple of Muslim houses at the bottom of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then? Were they detained there or were they allowed to move around freely? Did they have any escorts? Describe what you saw to us.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The Muslims would spend the night in these several houses and two of our men from the village would watch over them during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: For safety reasons, to prevent anything happening to them, because somebody unknown coming to the village might have done something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened in the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: During the day the Muslims went back to their own homes and went on with their daily duties, attending to their livestock, sowing things in their plot of land and so on, and they moved around the village quite normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time elapsed before you noticed that they were no longer in the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: About 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who organised their departure and how this was organised and why?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, I do not. Their departure was organised, but as they were all down at the bottom of the village, the part that I did not go to, I don't know who organised their departure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take in any refugees into the village later on?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which and where from?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: From Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, after the war, did the Muslims return, those of them who had lived in Gacice before the war?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims rebuilt the houses that -- their houses that had been destroyed. They had not been completely destroyed, but they repaired their houses and they all returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That completes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Let me turn to the Office of the Prosecutor for the cross-examination of the witness. Mr. Harmon, will it be you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, good morning Judge Shahabuddeen, good morning counsel, and good morning Mrs. Matic. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could start by putting this aerial image on the easel. And while that is being done, I will ask Mrs. Matic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put it on an easel. Actually, there is no easel here. About how much time are you going to need, Mr. Harmon, so that we can organise this morning's work?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would say at least half an hour to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. How long did the direct examination take, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I need some time in order to figure it out. Not very long, in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, what I am going to do is I am going to put an aerial image on the easel next to you. Mr. Usher, if you would put the whole image up. I will come over there and I will orient you and then I would like to ask you to identify where your house was located. Have you seen this image before?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me come over there, and I will probably be joined by my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, and I would like to orient you on this image so it will assist in identifying where your house was located. May I, Mr. President, approach the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And I would like to ask that the map be projected so that the public gallery can see it. Mr. Nobilo, if you want to approach the easel, you may, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, let me just orient you on this village, on this image. This is the town of Vitez, this is the factory, as you will see, here is the smoke stack with smoke coming up. This is the village of Gacice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please speak louder, Mr. Harmon, so that the interpreters can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I will raise my voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the village of Vitez, the village of Gacice, this is the factory about which you spoke, and this is Donje Veceriska. And you will see a number of roads, perhaps, come up into the village. What I would like you to do, please, is take a look at this for a minute or two and please tell us where your house was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Harmon. I'm trying to make this map match. It seems to me some of it was upside down or it was backwards. Can you show me where Vitez is, please? And Gacice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't hear you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And Gacice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right here. This is the factory right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. So that I can make the match with the two -- with the map.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, you will have to speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, it's very difficult for the interpreters to work under those conditions. Mr. Dubuisson and Mr. Usher, perhaps you can have a portable microphone brought over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point out your house?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: You said that this was the factory, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat your answer. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: You said that this was the factory, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the factory. This is a large smoke stack at the factory. This is smoke coming out of that smoke stack.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I cannot exactly tell whether my house is by this crossroads or that crossroads. I have trouble with this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live far from the location where the Muslims who had been taken to Vitez and were returned to Vitez were housed? Did you live near that part of the village or did you live in another part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: My house is near the crossroads, about 20 metres away from the road, and 20 metres on the other side of the road is the distance from that intersection to where the Muslim houses begin. And the Muslims, where were they? They were in a couple of houses, at the end of the village facing Vitez, but I am having trouble with this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try to assist you further, and if we can't make any progress, then we will abandon this effort. But let me assist you. This is Vitez and this is the road that came down into your village, the main road that came up into your village. Can you please tell me, as you came up the main road, where you lived? Did you live to the right, did you turn left on the main road?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: From the main road, the centre of the village, I think this is here. If this is the road from Vitez, leading from Vitez to Gacice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Then the Muslims were staying somewhere around here, in these houses, and then my house would be somewhere around here. I keep sticking to the crossroads on this map too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I need some additional clarification. Did you live in the upper part of the village or did you live in the lower part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The upper part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't get a translation.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The upper part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because, obviously, I have a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We don't have to dwell on this point too much. Madam, take your time in order to find a location of your house. It's an aerial photo. If you can't find it -- Mr. Harmon, perhaps you could move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, if we could have just one or two more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Unless, of course, it's very important for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to, looking at this map, Mrs. Matic, are you able to tell us where your house approximately was located, considering that this is the main road that comes up from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes. If this is the main road, then my house could be somewhere around here or here. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put just a circle in the general area where you think your house was approximately located. That's very faint, so I am going to take this pen and I am going to mark around that circle, and you tell me if I've correctly marked. Is it in that area, approximately, where your house was located?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think so. Although I am having quite a bit of trouble with this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I think that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you turn around, and I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Congratulations, Madam. It's not an easy task. All right. Mr. Harmon, ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate your taking the effort, Mrs. Matic, to work through that map. I know it's difficult. Mrs. Matic, let me start by taking your testimony in the order in which you gave it. You said that at some point in time two anti-aircraft guns were stolen from a location in your village. Can you give me the date or the approximate date when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that was four or five months earlier. I do not know exactly. It was the end of '92. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where, in fact, those guns ended up?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: As far as I managed to find out, in Vitez, in the Muslim section, in the Mahala that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if they remained in the Muslim section in Mahala in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's true, is it not, Mrs. Matic, that on the road that led to Gacice, in April, before the conflict started, there was a HVO checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: A checkpoint? A local checkpoint? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that checkpoint was manned by HVO soldiers, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Our people from the village were there at the checkpoint. They took turns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, were any Muslims at that particular checkpoint manning the checkpoint, or were they only Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't understand whether you are asking me about before the conflict or after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you before April 16th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that checkpoint were there only people who were Croats who manned that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Muslims man that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I simply don't understand. What date are you asking me about? The Muslims did not man anything with the Croats after the guns had been stolen, and after the conflict there were none left in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think, then, to just clarify, after the guns were stolen, the two anti-aircraft guns were stolen, some four or five months before the conflict started, the checkpoint that was at the base --

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- of your village was not manned by Muslims; is that correct? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said, in your testimony, that on the 16th of April you could hear shooting in Donje Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you hear that shooting? What was the first shooting that you heard?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that shooting in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that --

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Beginning of the day, yes. The morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the beginning of the day, you mean at dusk?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. No. I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you answer, Madam, would you please turn to the Judges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to the events that took place immediately after the 16th of April in your village. You testified that our people, meaning, I assume, the Bosnian Croats, selected a representative. Who was that representative that you selected?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Anto Krizanovic was the representative on the Croatian side and Kadir Hrustic on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in those discussions or negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you testified that both sides asked that arms be surrendered, you weren't present at those negotiations, were you?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Bosnian Croat side demanded and gave an ultimatum to the Muslims to surrender their arms within 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know exactly what was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that a counterproposal to that ultimatum by the Muslims was that both sides disarm and that that was rejected by the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to the 20th of April. I take it that at around 7.00 in the morning when you first heard two or three strong detonations, you were in your house?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you in your house when you heard the detonations, the first detonations?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I was in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: And then we fled to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what the source of those detonations was? Did you see if it was a mortar? Did you see if it was a rocket? Did you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see where those detonations exploded or those shells exploded?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the source, who fired the shells that caused the detonations?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know whether it was the Croats or the Muslims who fired those shells?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your house, you said you were present, your husband's brother was present, and your brother and sister-in-law and three children. Were there any weapons, any kind of a weapon, any rifle --

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- or any pistol in your house?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the two or three large detonations took place, did you and all members, who I have just identified as being in your house, go down into the basement?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the basement, if you can recall, until you first came up to kind of look around?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: They all stayed almost throughout, but I was the one who went to the window most often, and once, I went to the door, and then I never went out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, from your testimony, you went upstairs, am I correct and correct me if I'm wrong, on two occasions that morning?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: From the basement to the kitchen, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I went to the kitchen several times, but outside, I tried to go out only once when I saw these men with a canister, and as soon as they started shooting at me, I never went out again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the amount of time you spent out of the basement on the 20th of April could be calculated in a matter of minutes?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The time I spent outside the basement, you mean, in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: It would be very short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The time that you spent outside, you said you went outside briefly, was that also very short? Was that a matter of minutes?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: That was a matter of seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Other than that, you spent the remainder of the 20th in your basement until, I take it, let me just find out, until approximately what time?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you remain in the basement then until approximately 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. when you heard someone shouting, "Left wing. We're winning."

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, I was in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you first came up into the kitchen from the basement after you heard the detonations, you said you saw smoke at one end of the village.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain the origin of that smoke?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No, this smoke was in the lower part of the village, but later on, I found out that first it was Franjo Matic's haystack that was on fire. He was a Croat. But when I originally saw the smoke, I didn't know what was on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you just a few questions about the village of Gacice. You said it was about 50 per cent Muslim, 50 per cent Croat?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the village separated so that there was a Muslim part of the village and a Croat part of the village or did the Muslims and Croats have houses that were in between each other?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Part of the village was purely Muslim, and the rest was all mixed. There were Croat and Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where was the all-Muslim part of the village? Was it in the upper part, the lower part, the middle of the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The upper part of the village, across the road from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time was it that you saw a Muslim with a white flag?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Perhaps around 5.00. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that before 5.00 in the late afternoon of the 20th of April, a large group of Muslim civilians had already been taken down to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a large group of Muslims being taken down to Vitez on the 20th of April or were you in your basement when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: When the Muslims passed by with a white flag, they passed by my house, and I saw them, and I only heard that they took them to Vitez, but I could not see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know whether the group that you saw at 5.00 or 6.00 was the group that was going down to Vitez or whether a group of Muslims had already been taken down to Vitez, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, when you came out around 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon of the 20th and you saw that soldiers from the Bosnian Croat side were in the village, could you identify to what units of the HVO those soldiers belonged?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I heard them saying that they were Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you heard somebody say that they were Vitezovi. Did you also see on the 20th of April, 1993 soldiers who had HVO patches on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of patches they had. To tell you the truth, I wasn't watching their insignia or patches. I saw that they had camouflage uniforms, and I went there to put out the fire, and I didn't really look at these patches of theirs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, Mrs. Matic, you knew that some of the local people, some of the local Croats, in your village were members of the HVO, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, the people of the village had organised themselves, and what their name was, I mean, at first, there weren't any other military people from the outside in our village, that is to say, until the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you knew, did you not, that some people in your village were members of the army, the Bosnian Croat army, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know that they were in the army, people from our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any Bosnian Croat from the village of Gacice, prior to the conflict on April 16th, wearing a camouflage uniform and in possession of military arms?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was your village? How many people lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I said that there's about 100 houses, and how many people there are in the village, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that, of the Bosnian Croats in your village who were of military age, none of them were in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that they were members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the soldiers that you saw then at 5.00 or 6.00 on the afternoon of the 20th of April when they came through your village, the ones who were saying, "Left wing forward. We're winning," were those soldiers who were in the camouflage uniforms from outside the village? Were they people who didn't live in your village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read you some names, and I'm going to ask you if these people were in the HVO. Goran Strukar, son of Ante.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Goran Strukar, son of Ante, was taken prisoner by the Muslims as he was cutting grass for hay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question really is very simple. I'm going to read you some names, and I'm going to ask you if these people were members of the HVO, and all you have to do is, if you know them and you know the answer, you can say "yes" or "no." So let me read you some names, and let me ask you if these people were members of the HVO. Stipo Krizanovic.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Stipo Krizanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object. We would like to know the date when this list was made out. Actually, after the conflict, everybody was mobilised, so what does the question pertain to, to the period before the conflict or after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The conflict itself, April 16th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There's the answer, Mr. Nobilo. It's a relevant question, and there's the question. So you're speaking about April of 1993; is that correct, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to add a question. Isn't this going to cause a problem, that is, citing all these names?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't intend to cite many, Mr. President. I intend to cite people whom I believe were members of the HVO and just to verify this with this witness. These are people this witness should know. They were villagers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Ask your questions. Ask the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stipo Krizanovic, was that person a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know. These are young men from our village, but they probably were members of the HVO, but I don't know since when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you don't know, just say, "I don't know." "Yes," "no," or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There's some confusion. Let me go very slowly for the reporter as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Goran Strukar?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Boro Krizanovic, son of Vlado?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ivica Matic, called Iko, son of Nikola?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you had sons, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then who is Ride Matic, son of Franjo?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Oh, that's Franjo Matic, there's an elderly man who is also called that. I have two daughters, but my husband's name is also Franjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about Ride, R-I-D-E, Matic. Was that man in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jozo Matic, son of Ivo?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Jozo Matic, son of Ivo, worked in the police force. Whether he was a member or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zlatko Matic, son of Marko?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about our people in April, whether they were members or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zoran Matic, son of Marko?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dragan Matic, son of Marijan?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. The witness said that, "For our people," that is to say, she means the Croats, "I don't know whether they were soldiers before the conflict." Therefore, it is superfluous to read out the names when she said she did not know whether they were in the HVO before the conflict. We're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of course we're wasting some time, but don't try to take the place of your colleague, Mr. Harmon, but I would like to recall that the direct examination lasted for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm trying to get through this list as fast as I can, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I recognise that I interrupted you, but it was a good cause. I can see that Mr. Cayley is already wriggling with impatience to get to his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vinko Matic?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Srecko Krizanovic, son of Pero?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know where our people were in that particular month, whether they belonged to the HVO or not. Afterwards, they did, but whether they did at the time, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, Mrs. Matic: I won't read you the complete list, because I take your answer at its face value --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that would be long, and I will not accept having the entire list read. One last question on these names, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of those young men of military age in your village participate in the attack on the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you testified in direct examination in response to a question of my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, you said that the Muslims who had been fighting in the village fled through the forest, and the HVO intentionally left a space open through which the Muslim fighters could pass. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: It was told after the fighting was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it told --

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: It was recounted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it recounted by one of these young men in the village who was a Bosnian Croat of military age?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who spoke about this. There were groups of men and women, and everybody was commenting on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified about the death of Fikret Hrustic who, you said, drank a lot of alcohol, a lot of liquor. Did you see Fikret Hrustic on the 20th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he had been drinking on the 20th of April, 1993 when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him killed and do you know the circumstances under which he was killed?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the Muslims who had returned to the village of Gacice were put in a certain limited number of houses, and they were free to move around during the day. Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go down and visit those Muslims in those houses while they were detained in them?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to any of those Muslims who were detained in your village about the conditions under which they were being held?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
