utterances.text: Are you aware that approximately 267 Muslims were put on trucks, driven to a checkpoint near the Dubravica school and told to walk to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I heard that they had left, but how they left and where they went to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not aware then that the HVO put them on trucks and took them to the Dubravica school and told them to walk to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you some other questions. Do you know a man by the name of Sabahet Herceg? He was called Car.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Sabahet Herceg?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I know a Sabahet Herceg, but they call him Car, the Car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had a small shop located near where you lived, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to his shop after the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened. I know that his house was knocked down, and that is near my brother, where the facilities were on fire. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that his shop was completely looted and all the goods in it were taken away, and yet you lived only a short distance from that shop and remained in the village of Gacice after the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: My house is about 100 metres away from his house and his shop. How do I know what happened there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you another question then, Mrs. Matic. Did Mr. Herceg also have a tractor?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, that Sabahet Herceg did not have a tractor. His uncle had a tractor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what happened to that tractor.

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: The uncle of Sabahet Herceg had left the tractor with a Croat, and after the conflict, he gave the tractor back to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, after the Muslims left the village of Gacice on the 20th, acquire any Muslim property?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you acquire a tractor that belonged to Sabahet Herceg?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No. What would I do with a tractor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the death of a young man, and his name, if you give me just a minute, was Ekrem Hercegovac. I think I've pronounced his name right. Was he one of the young men who was killed in the village on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Ekrem Herceg was not a young man. He was about 50 years old at the time. I heard that he had been killed at the end of the village, but I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody on the 20th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if you have important questions, go ahead, because time is moving on. You've gone quite beyond the time that was used for the direct examination. Get to the essential points, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will. I only have a few more minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody from your house, on the 20th of April, 1993, shoot out of your house and shoot toward any of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, in respect of the attack on your village, are you aware that before the attack there was a rocket launcher that was placed near the graveyard in the village? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about a large recoilless rifle, are you aware that that was also placed in your village near the houses, the Garica houses? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you aware of a rocket launcher that was down in the factory, the factory that was adjacent to your village, and that it was positioned there before the attack? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Before the attack, nothing was positioned there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, one of the last areas I'd like to ask you about is, the area where the Muslims were detained in those limited number of houses that you've described was across from a Muslim cemetery, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that, during the time that the Muslims were there, there was a large earth remover that dug a long trench along the side of the cemetery, inside the cemetery? Do you remember seeing that?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that victims of the attack on Ahmici were buried in that particular cemetery?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your examination-in-chief that certain refugees from Zenica had come to your village. Were those refugees Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, thank you very much. I appreciate your co-operation and assistance. Mr. President, I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a break. Mr. Nobilo, do you have any clarifications you want to bring?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just two questions. Only two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's your right. It's your right. I thought that Mr. Harmon had taken too much time, but that doesn't mean I want to shorten your time. I am simply asking whether you had any questions to ask. If you do, go ahead. I think that perhaps we should take a break after the witness answers the final questions. Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Matic, about the young men from your village before the beginning of the conflict, before the 20th of April, do you know whether they were only members of the village watch or whether they were members of the HVO as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I think they were only members of the village watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the start of the conflict, did all the men then become, in the course of 1993, members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The civilians that you saw in the village, did you think they were prisoners or did you see them moving freely around the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: They moved freely around the village and worked, and when they left, I don't know whether they wanted to leave of their own free will or not, but many of them left their belongings with the Croats. And these belongings were looked after and returned to them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any violence against those individuals or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, I think you said that you looked out and you recognised some Muslim men wearing checkerboard insignia and carrying containers which they used to attack Croat houses. Do you recall your evidence to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you recognised some Muslim men in your village who were attacking Croats. Did you recognise any Croat men from your village who were attacking Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I did not recognise any Muslims attacking. I recognised the three Muslim men who were carrying the containers and setting fire to our buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well then, do forgive me if I refer to that by speaking of Muslim men who were attacking Croats. Did you recognise any Croat men from your village who were in any way involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: When I saw a group of the army who said, "Left wing forward, the victory is ours," I don't know whether there was anybody there who was a Croat from the village, because they weren't close enough to me for me to be able to recognise them. Whereas around the village, apart from those who set fire to the buildings, I did not see either Croats or Muslims. Quite simply, nobody moved around the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us turn, briefly, to Mr. Fikret Hrustic who died in his building. Is my recollection correct that your evidence was to the effect that he was burnt alive in his house?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I did not say he was burnt alive. I said he was burnt, burnt in his house. His house is right next to a Croatian house and the family from the Croat house entreated him to leave his house, because they knew he was a harmless man, and that he would only have to step out of his house and nothing would happen to him. However, I heard tell, I wasn't there, but I heard tell that either he did not dare or did not want to leave. A shot was heard and flames were seen. Later on they said that he had a rifle and that was why he did not dare leave the house. Now, how the fire actually started, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is it your impression that he was already dead or that he was alive when his house was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You don't know. Now, you spoke of a group of Muslims who left the village after a while, and I think you said you did not know who organised their departure. I am trying to locate you in your evidence. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mrs. Matic, did you inquire as to who might have organised their departure from the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, then finally let us talk a little about these two guns. I think you said they were anti-aircraft guns which were stolen or removed by the Muslims. They were removed by the Muslims from whom?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, they were taken from that place where they were, without any agreement reached with the Croats. They took them away during the night. That's what I heard, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Who had the guns before they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I think, as far as I know, they were guns from the factory which were positioned because of the Serbian planes which, very often, flew over our factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, that tells us where the guns came from and what purpose they were intended to serve. I ask you who had the guns before they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Probably owned by the factory. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were there any people on the site who were controlling the guns?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were they Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Both. I see. Now, after the guns were taken, did the Croats have any guns, any anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: ANDZELKA MATIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Thank you Mrs. Matic. That's all. You can be released now. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom. We would again like to express our gratitude to you for having come to The Hague. The Judges will suspend the session now. Let me turn to Mr. Kehoe. Do you think that during the next sequence, we won't talk about that here because of the closed session issue, but how much time do you think you will need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can finish it certainly in the next sequence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Because we finish at 1.30. There might be some additional questions. All right. We are going to -- I see Mr. Dubuisson is saying something to me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I simply want to know what is to be done with the Prosecutor exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was going to ask that that be marked as an exhibit and that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We would like to tender the last exhibit, D520, but also the previous one, D519, and then as regards D517 and 518, we suggest that they be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Any comments from either of the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to 517 and 518, I do believe that until we get a full translation of the entire book, I just would ask that most respectfully we hold that in abeyance. There may be no objection, I just would like to see those documents in context with the entire book once it's translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. For the time being we will only give them numbers and wait until the translation has been done. I hope you keep a very careful count of these documents, because at the end of the proceedings we have to decide what has to be done with all of the pending documents. I would like to remind you, Mr. Kehoe, that the two documents in issue, I am talking about parts of documents, and that it is very infrequent that a demand is made for the translation of an entire document before the document is tendered. You yourself at times asked that three lines of a military communique be admitted, and whereas the eight pages of military communique in which the text was found, for example, Colonel Watters, we didn't ask that we wait until the translation was done. I am willing to do so, but I would like to say that my concern is that at the end of the proceedings the registrar will have to go back to the entire list of all of the exhibits so that the Judges deliberations can be done based on an agreement between the parties in respect of all of the exhibits. So when you ask for complete translation of documents, that becomes the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So how do you feel about the need for the translation of the entire thing? What is your opinion? Do you have to have the whole document translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would like, because I would like to see this in context with everything else, and I think it's significant that these particular provisions that have been taken and translated at the request of the Defence be looked at in conjunction with the rest of the matters, which could very well necessitate -- well, we can talk about that in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The registrar suggests that they could be admitted subject to. All right. We are going to take a 20-minute break, because the interpreters have done a lot of work. Do you want to add something, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just that I think the two exhibits, 517 and 518, they are either under seal or they are open to the public, and depending on a request for a change by the Prosecutor, we ask that they be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. All right, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection to those documents being placed under seal, and we have no objection to the admission of 519 and 520.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. We'll take a 20-minute break. Let me remind you, Mr. Kehoe, that we will finish at 1.30. You have 20 minutes for the cross-examination, and there could be 10 minutes of redirect, and we will be finished at 1.30. This is a decision. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume in closed session. Have the accused brought in. (Closed session) (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th of January, 1999 at 10.00 a.m. 25
